---
title: "Atomic Layer Deposition"
---

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## Learning outcomes
After this chapter you should be able to:

1. State the operational definition of ALD and design an experiment that tests it.
2. Write the two half-reactions of the TMA/H~2~O model process and explain how they alternate in one cycle.
3. Explain why the GPC of TMA/H~2~O is a fraction of a monolayer, using the fundamentals in @sec-saturation.
:::

## What makes a process ALD? {#sec-what-makes-ald}

Atomic layer deposition builds a film by exposing a surface to two (or more) reactants **one at a time**, with a purge or evacuation between them. Each exposure is a gas–surface reaction that stops by itself once the available surface sites are used up [@George2010; @Johnson2014].

The defining property is **self-limitation**, not the cycle structure. Plenty of pulsed processes have an A–purge–B–purge sequence but are not ALD, because one of the steps keeps depositing material as the dose increases. The practical test is therefore experimental:

> For each half-reaction, the growth per cycle (GPC) must reach a plateau as that reactant's dose increases, and must not depend on purge length once the purge is adequate.

Any other characteristic (conformality, digital thickness control, low pinhole density) follows from this property. None of them can stand in for testing it.

## The model system: TMA/H~2~O → Al~2~O~3~ {#sec-tma-model}

The trimethylaluminum (TMA)/water process is the most-studied ALD chemistry and is the usual reference point [@Puurunen2005]. In simplified form, the two half-reactions on a hydroxylated surface (asterisks denote surface species) are:

$$
\text{A:}\quad \|\!-\!\text{OH}^* + \text{Al(CH}_3)_3 \rightarrow \|\!-\!\text{O–Al(CH}_3)_2^* + \text{CH}_4
$$ {#eq-tma}

$$
\text{B:}\quad \|\!-\!\text{Al–CH}_3^* + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \|\!-\!\text{Al–OH}^* + \text{CH}_4
$$ {#eq-water}

Reaction A consumes hydroxyls and leaves a methyl-terminated surface that does not react further with TMA. Reaction B restores the hydroxyl termination. The overall reaction, 2 Al(CH~3~)~3~ + 3 H~2~O → Al~2~O~3~ + 6 CH~4~, is strongly exothermic, which partly explains why the process is so robust [@George2010].

Step through one cycle below to see how the two half-reactions alternate. The diagram is a cartoon: each dot is an atom, but sizes and spacings are not to scale.

[Simulation 3.1: One ALD cycle of TMA/H~2~O]{.sim-title}

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof cyc = {
  const wrap = html`<div class="cycle-controls">
    <button type="button" data-a="prev" aria-label="Previous step">◀ Back</button>
    <button type="button" data-a="play" aria-label="Play or pause">▶ Play</button>
    <button type="button" data-a="next" aria-label="Next step">Next ▶</button>
    <button type="button" data-a="reset" aria-label="Reset to start">Reset</button>
  </div>`;
  let v = 0, timer = null;
  const playBtn = wrap.querySelector('[data-a="play"]');
  const set = (x) => {
    v = Math.max(0, Math.min(x, 400));
    wrap.value = v;
    wrap.dispatchEvent(new Event("input", {bubbles: true}));
  };
  const stop = () => { clearInterval(timer); timer = null; playBtn.textContent = "▶ Play"; };
  wrap.value = v;
  wrap.setTo = (x) => { stop(); set(x); };
  wrap.addEventListener("click", (e) => {
    const a = e.target.closest("button")?.dataset.a;
    if (a === "next") { stop(); set(v + 1); }
    if (a === "prev") { stop(); set(v - 1); }
    if (a === "reset") { stop(); set(0); }
    if (a === "play") {
      if (timer) stop();
      else { playBtn.textContent = "❚❚ Pause"; set(v + 1); timer = setInterval(() => set(v + 1), 2200); }
    }
  });
  invalidation.then(stop);
  return wrap;
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
cycleFigure = {
  const GPC = 1.1;                                     // Å, for the thickness readout
  const step = cyc === 0 ? -1 : (cyc - 1) % 4;         // -1 = starting surface
  const cycleNo = cyc === 0 ? 1 : Math.floor((cyc - 1) / 4) + 1;
  const done = Math.floor(cyc / 4);                    // completed cycles
  const steps = [
    {name: "Pulse TMA", short: "TMA", gas: "Al(CH₃)₃"},
    {name: "Purge", short: "Purge", gas: "N₂"},
    {name: "Pulse H₂O", short: "H₂O", gas: "H₂O"},
    {name: "Purge", short: "Purge", gas: "N₂"}
  ];
  const red = "#E91C24", dark = "#4D4D4D", grey = "#8C8C8C", light = "#EDEDED";

  // --- atoms --------------------------------------------------------------
  const atom = (x, y, el, r) => {
    const s = {Al: [dark, "white", 11], O: [red, "white", 9], C: ["#000", "white", 9],
               H: ["white", "#000", 5.5], N: [grey, "white", 7]}[el];
    const rr = r ?? s[2];
    const lab = el === "H" ? "" : `<text x="${x}" y="${y + 3.5}" text-anchor="middle" font-size="${el === "Al" ? 10 : 9.5}" fill="${s[1]}" font-weight="600">${el === "C" ? "C" : el}</text>`;
    return `<circle cx="${x}" cy="${y}" r="${rr}" fill="${s[0]}" stroke="#000" stroke-width="${el === "H" ? 1 : 0.8}"/>${lab}`;
  };
  const bond = (x1, y1, x2, y2) => `<line x1="${x1}" y1="${y1}" x2="${x2}" y2="${y2}" stroke="#000" stroke-width="1.4"/>`;
  // Carbon with explicit H atoms. A methyl's three H point away from the atom it is bonded to (ax, ay).
  const withH = (x, y, angles) => {
    const hs = angles.map(a => [x + 14 * Math.cos(a), y + 14 * Math.sin(a)]);
    return hs.map(([hx, hy]) => bond(x, y, hx, hy)).join("") + hs.map(([hx, hy]) => atom(hx, hy, "H")).join("") + atom(x, y, "C");
  };
  const methyl = (x, y, ax, ay) => {
    const d = Math.atan2(y - ay, x - ax), s = 1.1;
    return withH(x, y, [d - s, d, d + s]);
  };
  const tma = (x, y) => bond(x, y, x - 20, y + 12) + bond(x, y, x + 20, y + 12) + bond(x, y, x, y - 23) +
    methyl(x - 20, y + 12, x, y) + methyl(x + 20, y + 12, x, y) + methyl(x, y - 23, x, y) + atom(x, y, "Al");
  const water = (x, y) => bond(x, y, x - 10, y + 8) + bond(x, y, x + 10, y + 8) + atom(x - 10, y + 8, "H") + atom(x + 10, y + 8, "H") + atom(x, y, "O");
  const methane = (x, y) => withH(x, y, [0.785, 2.356, 3.927, 5.498]);
  const n2 = (x, y) => atom(x - 6, y, "N", 6) + atom(x + 6, y, "N", 6);

  // --- reactor geometry -----------------------------------------------------
  const X0 = 250, X1 = 720, GAS_TOP = 30, SUB_TOP = 330;
  const filmPx = Math.min(done, 12) * 5;               // drawn film thickness
  const surf = SUB_TOP - filmPx;                       // top of film
  const sites = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5].map(i => 285 + i * 78);
  // Adsorbed species after the TMA pulse. "di": TMA on one –OH (–O–Al(CH₃)₂);
  // "mono": TMA bridging two –OH (–O)₂Al(CH₃); "oh": –OH shielded by neighbouring methyls.
  const species = [
    {type: "di", at: [0]}, {type: "mono", at: [1, 2]}, {type: "di", at: [3]},
    {type: "oh", at: [4]}, {type: "di", at: [5]}
  ];

  // surface state after the current step
  const state = step === 0 || step === 1 ? "Me" : step === 2 ? "OH" : "bare";
  const lig = (x, y, ax, ay) => state === "Me" ? methyl(x, y, ax, ay) : bond(x, y, x, y - 16) + atom(x, y - 16, "H") + atom(x, y, "O");
  const tags = {di: "dimethyl", mono: "monomethyl", oh: "shielded –OH"};
  let surface = "";
  const y0 = surf - 9, yAl = y0 - 26;
  species.forEach(sp => {
    const xs = sp.at.map(i => sites[i]);
    if (state === "bare" || sp.type === "oh") {
      xs.forEach(x => { surface += bond(x, y0, x, y0 - 16) + atom(x, y0 - 16, "H") + atom(x, y0, "O"); });
    } else if (sp.type === "di") {
      const x = xs[0];
      surface += bond(x, y0, x, yAl) + bond(x, yAl, x - 16, yAl - 18) + bond(x, yAl, x + 16, yAl - 18) +
        lig(x - 16, yAl - 18, x, yAl) + lig(x + 16, yAl - 18, x, yAl) + atom(x, yAl, "Al") + atom(x, y0, "O");
    } else {
      const xm = (xs[0] + xs[1]) / 2;
      surface += xs.map(x => bond(x, y0, xm, yAl)).join("") + bond(xm, yAl, xm, yAl - 20) +
        lig(xm, yAl - 20, xm, yAl) + atom(xm, yAl, "Al") + xs.map(x => atom(x, y0, "O")).join("");
    }
    if (step === 0 || step === 1) {
      const xm = xs.reduce((u, v) => u + v, 0) / xs.length;
      surface += `<text x="${xm}" y="${surf - (sp.type === "oh" ? 52 : 82)}" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="${dark}">${tags[sp.type]}</text>`;
    }
  });

  // gas phase
  const P = [[300, 88], [395, 130], [480, 96], [560, 140], [655, 95], [345, 185], [615, 195], [500, 205]];
  const g = (f, idx) => idx.map((k, j) => `<g class="drift" style="animation-delay:${-j * 0.7}s">${f(P[k][0], P[k][1])}</g>`).join("");
  let gas = "";
  if (step === 0) gas = g(tma, [0, 2, 4, 5]) + g(methane, [1, 3, 6, 7]);
  if (step === 1 || step === 3) gas = g(n2, [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]);
  if (step === 2) gas = g(water, [0, 2, 4, 5, 7]) + g(methane, [1, 3, 6]);

  const flowLabel = step === -1 ? "" : steps[step].gas;
  const reactor = `
    <rect x="${X0}" y="${GAS_TOP}" width="${X1 - X0}" height="${SUB_TOP - GAS_TOP}" fill="#FFFFFF" stroke="${grey}"/>
    ${step >= 0 ? `<g class="flow"><path d="M${X0 + 8} 22 h60" stroke="${step % 2 ? grey : red}" stroke-width="3" marker-end="url(#arr)"/></g>
       <text x="${X0 + 8}" y="16" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="${step % 2 ? dark : red}">in: ${flowLabel}</text>
       <text x="${X1 - 8}" y="16" font-size="12" text-anchor="end" fill="${dark}">to pump →</text>` : ""}
    <rect x="${X0}" y="${SUB_TOP}" width="${X1 - X0}" height="28" fill="${light}" stroke="${grey}"/>
    <text x="${X1 - 8}" y="${SUB_TOP + 18}" font-size="11" text-anchor="end" fill="${dark}">substrate</text>
    ${filmPx ? `<rect x="${X0}" y="${surf}" width="${X1 - X0}" height="${filmPx}" fill="#F4B6B8" stroke="${red}" stroke-width="0.6"/>` : ""}
    ${gas}${surface}`;

  // --- cycle ring -------------------------------------------------------------
  const cx = 115, cy = 150, R = 82, w = 26;
  const arc = (k) => {
    const a0 = -Math.PI / 2 + k * Math.PI / 2 + 0.06, a1 = a0 + Math.PI / 2 - 0.12;
    const p = (a, r) => [cx + r * Math.cos(a), cy + r * Math.sin(a)];
    const [x0, y0] = p(a0, R), [x1, y1] = p(a1, R), [x2, y2] = p(a1, R - w), [x3, y3] = p(a0, R - w);
    const on = k === step;
    const fill = on ? red : k % 2 ? light : "#D6D6D6";
    const am = (a0 + a1) / 2, [lx, ly] = p(am, R + 16);
    const anchor = Math.cos(am) > 0.2 ? "start" : Math.cos(am) < -0.2 ? "end" : "middle";
    return `<g class="ring-step" data-k="${k}" style="cursor:pointer">
      <path d="M${x0},${y0} A${R},${R} 0 0 1 ${x1},${y1} L${x2},${y2} A${R - w},${R - w} 0 0 0 ${x3},${y3} Z" fill="${fill}" stroke="#fff" stroke-width="2"/>
      <text x="${lx}" y="${ly + 4}" text-anchor="${anchor}" font-size="13.5" font-weight="${on ? 700 : 400}" fill="${on ? red : "#000"}">${k + 1}. ${steps[k].short}</text></g>`;
  };
  const ring = [0, 1, 2, 3].map(arc).join("") + `
    <text x="${cx}" y="${cy - 6}" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" font-weight="600">Cycle ${cycleNo}</text>
    <text x="${cx}" y="${cy + 13}" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="${dark}">${done} done · ≈ ${(done * GPC).toFixed(1)} Å</text>`;

  // --- valve timing strip ----------------------------------------------------------
  const TX = 250, TW = 470, TY = 385, seg = TW / 4;
  const trace = (row, k, label, col) => {
    const y = TY + row * 30, hi = y - 12;
    const xs = TX + k * seg;
    return `<text x="${TX - 8}" y="${y + 2}" text-anchor="end" font-size="12.5" fill="${dark}">${label}</text>
      <path d="M${TX},${y} H${xs + 6} V${hi} H${xs + seg - 6} V${y} H${TX + TW}" fill="none" stroke="${col}" stroke-width="2"/>`;
  };
  const timing = `
    ${step >= 0 ? `<rect x="${TX + step * seg}" y="${TY - 24}" width="${seg}" height="56" fill="${red}" opacity="0.1"/>` : ""}
    ${trace(0, 0, "TMA valve", red)}${trace(1, 2, "H₂O valve", dark)}
    ${steps.map((s, k) => `<text x="${TX + k * seg + seg / 2}" y="${TY + 48}" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12.5" fill="${k === step ? red : dark}" font-weight="${k === step ? 700 : 400}">${s.name}</text>`).join("")}`;

  const key = `<g transform="translate(10,458)" font-size="12.5" fill="${dark}">
    <text x="0" y="0">Key:</text>
    ${atom(45, -4, "Al")}<text x="60" y="0">Al</text>
    ${atom(95, -4, "O")}<text x="108" y="0">O</text>
    ${methyl(152, -2, 152, 12)}<text x="176" y="0">methyl group (CH₃)</text>
    ${atom(302, -4, "H")}<text x="313" y="0">H</text>
    ${n2(345, -4)}<text x="360" y="0">N₂ purge gas</text>
    <rect x="465" y="-11" width="16" height="10" fill="#F4B6B8" stroke="${red}" stroke-width="0.6"/><text x="487" y="0">deposited Al₂O₃</text></g>`;
  const wrap = document.createElement("div");
  wrap.innerHTML = `<svg viewBox="0 0 740 470" width="100%" style="max-width:820px" role="img" aria-label="ALD cycle diagram, step ${step + 1}">
    <defs><marker id="arr" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="8" refY="5" markerWidth="6" markerHeight="6" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z" fill="context-stroke"/></marker></defs>
    ${ring}${reactor}${timing}${key}</svg>`;
  wrap.querySelectorAll(".ring-step").forEach(el => el.addEventListener("click", () => {
    const k = +el.dataset.k;
    viewof cyc.setTo(4 * (cycleNo - 1) + k + 1);
  }));
  return wrap;
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const step = cyc === 0 ? -1 : (cyc - 1) % 4;
  const text = [
    ["Starting surface", "A hydroxylated (–OH-terminated) substrate. Press <b>Next</b> or <b>Play</b>, or click a step in the ring."],
    ["1. Pulse TMA", "Al(CH₃)₃ reacts with surface –OH groups in two ways. Reacting with one –OH gives a <b>dimethyl</b> species, ‖–OH* + Al(CH₃)₃ → ‖–O–Al(CH₃)₂* + CH₄. Reacting with two neighbouring –OH groups gives a <b>monomethyl</b> species, 2 ‖–OH* + Al(CH₃)₃ → (‖–O)₂–Al(CH₃)* + 2 CH₄. The balance between the two sets how many methyl groups go on to the water step. Once the reachable –OH groups are used up, the methyl-terminated surface does not react with more TMA, so the half-reaction stops by itself. Some –OH groups stay unreacted because neighbouring methyl groups shield them (steric hindrance). Excess TMA and CH₄ remain in the gas."],
    ["2. Purge", "Inert gas sweeps out unreacted TMA and the CH₄ by-product. If the purge is too short, TMA meets water in the gas phase in the next step and CVD growth adds to the film."],
    ["3. Pulse H₂O", "Water converts every remaining surface methyl group, on both dimethyl and monomethyl species, to a hydroxyl: ‖–Al–CH₃* + H₂O → ‖–Al–OH* + CH₄. The surface is hydroxylated again and ready for the next TMA pulse."],
    ["4. Purge", "Water and CH₄ are removed. The cycle is complete, and the new Al–O material is now part of the film (pink). Each cycle adds about one GPC (≈ 1.1 Å), well below one monolayer of Al₂O₃."]
  ][step + 1];
  return html`<div class="map-card"><div class="map-card-title">${text[0]}</div><div>${html([text[1]])}</div></div>`;
}
```

::: {.assumptions}
**Assumptions.** Idealized chemistry: TMA binds to one –OH (dimethyl) or two –OH (monomethyl); dissociation onto Al–O bridges is left out, and water removes every remaining methyl group. The mix of dimethyl, monomethyl and unreacted sites is chosen for illustration; in reality it depends on temperature and –OH density. After each completed cycle the new material is drawn as a uniform film layer, and the thickness readout uses a fixed GPC of 1.1 Å. Pulse and purge times on the valve trace are schematic.
:::
:::

Two points are worth stating early, because students often get them wrong:

- **GPC is a fraction of a monolayer.** For TMA/H~2~O, a typical GPC is about 1 Å, which is well below the thickness of one "layer" of Al~2~O~3~. The amount of metal adsorbed per cycle is limited by **steric hindrance** from the ligands that remain after chemisorption and by the **number of reactive sites**. Which of the two dominates depends on the chemistry and the temperature [@Puurunen2005] (see @sec-steric).
- **Eqs. [-@eq-tma]–[-@eq-water] are idealized.** In reality, TMA can react with one or two hydroxyls, and it can also dissociate onto Al–O bridges. The ratio between these pathways sets how many methyl groups survive into step B. This is why the hydroxyl density, and hence the temperature, controls the GPC.

## Where the fundamentals are

The ideas that ALD shares with the other atomic layer processes are developed in @sec-saturation to @sec-surfaces, and this chapter does not repeat them. For ALD in particular:

- **Saturation and dose.** The rate equations, the Langmuir isotherm and the saturation curve are in @sec-ka-kd to @sec-saturation-curve; estimating the dose needed for a planar surface or a high-aspect-ratio structure is in @sec-dose.
- **Why GPC is a fraction of a monolayer.** Steric crowding by the TMA fragments, with a simulation of the TMA half-cycle and a worked conversion from GPC to coverage, is in @sec-steric.
- **The ALD window.** What the window means, and where the idea breaks down, is in @sec-ald-window.
- **Ligands, precursors and second precursors** are in @sec-ligands and @sec-precursors; thermal testing of precursors is in @sec-thermolysis.
- **Surface mechanisms**, including the TMA/O~3~ chemistry and the redox steps behind TiN and Cu, are in @sec-mechanisms.
- **Nucleation and initial growth**, including correcting a GPC estimate for a nucleation delay, are in @sec-surfaces and @sec-growth-modes.

## Check your understanding

::: {.quiz}
Doubling the TMA pulse time raises film thickness by 30 %, with everything else unchanged. What is the most defensible conclusion?

- [ ] The process is below the ALD window.
- [x] The TMA step is not self-limiting under these conditions; either it is undersaturated or there is a non-self-limiting contribution, and a full dose series is needed to tell which.
- [ ] The water half-reaction is undersaturated.
- [ ] The process is ALD; a 30 % change is within normal reactor variability.

::: {.explanation}
One pair of points cannot tell undersaturation (the GPC will plateau at longer pulses) apart from a decomposition or CVD component (the GPC keeps rising). Nothing here tests the water step or the temperature.
:::
:::

## Further reading

- @George2010: a broad overview of ALD chemistries and mechanisms.
- @Puurunen2005: the definitive case study of TMA/H~2~O surface chemistry and of GPC-limiting factors.
- @Johnson2014: a short, accessible review from fundamentals to applications.
